SOFTWARE ENGINEERING — 3 MIN READ

Your first pull request is a conversation.

Good code matters. So does how you explain it to the next person.

S.
SOC EditorialSample story

Your code works on your machine. You have checked the changes, taken a breath, and opened your first pull request. Now someone else has to understand what you changed—and, more importantly, why.

It helps to think of that request as the beginning of a conversation, not the delivery of a finished verdict. The code is one part of it. The context you give the reviewer is another.

Start with the problem.

A description that says “updated files” asks your reviewer to reconstruct your entire afternoon. A description that explains the broken behaviour, the intended outcome, and the approach you chose gives them somewhere useful to start.

Imagine a classmate opening the request between lectures. Can they tell what a user will experience differently? Can they see which part deserves the closest attention? Have you pointed out the thing you are still uncertain about?

Make it easy for someone to understand your thinking, not just inspect your typing.

Keep the conversation focused.

When a bug fix also renames half the project and changes the formatting of unrelated files, every extra change competes for attention. A small, coherent request is easier to discuss because its purpose stays visible.

This does not mean counting lines as a measure of quality. It means keeping the changes connected to the problem you are trying to solve. If a separate improvement can stand on its own, give it its own conversation.

Show what you checked.

Tell the reviewer how you checked the result. If you tried a particular input, describe it. If a layout changes, show the relevant state. If you could not check something, say so plainly. “I have not tested this on a slow connection” is more useful than an unqualified “works perfectly.”

Being precise about what you know is not a weakness. It gives your teammate a clear place to contribute instead of leaving them to guess what is missing.

Separate the feedback from yourself.

A question about a function is not a judgment on your future as an engineer. Read the question, check the context, and explain the choice. Sometimes your explanation will reveal that the code should change. Sometimes it will reveal that the reviewer needs information you forgot to include.

You can disagree respectfully. You can also say, “I had not considered that.” Both are part of learning to work with people.

The goal is not to make it through review untouched. The goal is for the shared work to become clearer, and for everyone involved to understand it a little better than they did before.
